title: Is this planning approach appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether a way of planning in a scenario is fit for purpose, and pick the reason that really explains the verdict.
question: At a stage boundary, Pinewick's project manager writes a task-by-task plan for every sprint of the next stage. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?

teach.h: Four tests for any planning decision
teach.body: When a question asks whether planning is fit for purpose, test it four ways. Level: is the detail in the right artifact, high level in the release map and task level in the team plan? Timing: is detail added just in time, not too early? Basis: does the forecast come from the team's own measured progress? People: are estimates relative and made by the whole team, and is work agreed between the PM and the product owner? A 'No' breaks one of these tests.

teach.body: In 'Is this appropriate, and why?' items, two options give each verdict. The wrong reasons are usually true statements about planning that do not explain this situation, such as 'the board approves the next stage plan' or 'velocity is empirical'. Ask: does this reason answer why THIS approach fits or fails? If it would be equally true of a different approach, it is probably the decoy.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile Practitioner syllabus (analyse criteria); PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.3

colHead: Reason true but beside the point
teach.caption: Settle the verdict from the scenario first; then choose between the two reasons on that row.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick's click and collect
teach.body: In initiation, project manager Patrick Dunne and Marcus Lindell, the chief product owner, build a story map with both teams and cluster it into three releases. A product flow diagram shows Tallis's stock interface must come first, so Release 1 is placed after Tallis's next quarterly release. The budget covers delivery and project management costs. When the finance director asks for every sprint planned in detail, Patrick explains that each team plans tasks for its next iteration, and forecasts use each team's own measured rate.

steps.label: Locate
steps.sub: Which process and which level of plan?

steps.label: Reason
steps.sub: Pick the one that explains this case

teach.text: Traps: 'the board approves the next stage plan' is true but does not justify task-level detail, because that plan is a high-level release map. 'Velocity is empirical' is true but does not justify using another team's velocity. Task planning happens in managing product delivery, not at the stage boundary. A single person's hour estimates are not whole-team relative estimates.

items: Fit for purpose = right artifact, right level, just in time, empirical, collaborative.
Stage boundaries update the high-level release map; teams plan tasks for the next iteration.
Forecast from the team's own velocity; rationalism and borrowed rates are poor fits.
The story map can replace the product breakdown structure; duplicating both is waste.
Pick the reason that explains the scenario, not a true statement beside the point.

summary: You can now judge whether a planning approach in a scenario is fit for purpose by testing its level, timing, basis and collaboration. You can also reject true-but-irrelevant reasons and choose the one that explains why the approach works or fails.

A.q: Easterholm County Council's Care Online project is in initiation. Project manager Simon Archer prepares the budget for the release map. It includes the costs of the digital team, the Abacus interface work and equipment, but leaves out the cost of the project management activities. Which change would MOST improve this plan?
options: Remove the Abacus costs, which belong in the commercial approach
Add the cost of the project management activities to the budget
Move the budget into each sprint's team plan for the digital team
Replace the budget with a forecast based on the team's velocity
A.why: Preparing the budget covers the costs of producing and delivering the products and the cost of the project management activities (8.3.1.5).

whyNot.0: The commercial management approach describes how suppliers are engaged; the supplier's costs still belong in the plan's budget.
whyNot.2: Team plans are task-level plans for the next iteration; the budget is included in or referenced by the release map.
whyNot.3: Velocity forecasts timing; it does not replace the budget, which plans must include or reference.

A.q: At Callowmere University, the head of the web team will not commit his team to any feature more than one sprint ahead. The pro vice-chancellor needs to know which features are expected in Release 1 before Welcome Week. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the team to plan every sprint to Welcome Week at task level
Leave release content open until each sprint has been finished
Keep a release map of features, and team plans a sprint ahead
Ask the chief product owner to set the team's velocity target
A.why: The release map shows which features are expected in each release at a high level, while the team plans tasks only for the next iteration (8.3.2.5, Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: Task-level plans for every sprint would be planning too early; detail is added just in time.
whyNot.1: The board still needs a high-level release map showing the expected features and timing.
whyNot.3: Velocity is measured from the team's actual progress; it is not a target set by the CPO.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's Smart Maintenance project is in initiation. Project manager Andrea Lucas creates a full product breakdown structure for the project and then a separate user story map that breaks the same products into stories. How well does this apply the plans practice, and why?
options: Well, because two views of the products add assurance
Well, because a PBS is required in product-based planning
Poorly, because a story map is built in closing a project
Poorly, because a story map can replace the separate PBS
A.why: PRINCE2 Agile recommends replacing the product breakdown structure with a user story map, which breaks products into stories and removes the need for a separate PBS (8.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: Two documents covering the same breakdown duplicate effort; the story map is meant to take the PBS's place.
whyNot.1: Product-based planning is tailored in agile: the story map is recommended in place of the PBS.
whyNot.2: Story maps support planning in starting up and initiation, not closing a project.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team is starting a new iteration. Project manager Sally Greaves sends the team a work package listing the tasks each person must complete on each day. Raj Malhotra prioritizes the team's work as its product owner. What should Sally agree instead?
options: A release map listing the tasks for each team member
A set of user stories agreed with the product owner
A project backlog of epics for the team to split up
A team plan drawn up by the project manager herself
B.why: In PRINCE2 Agile the work package description is a set of user stories agreed between the PM and the PO; the team then produces its own team plan (7.3.1, 8.3.2).

whyNot.0: The release map is a high-level plan of releases and features, not a task list for individuals.
whyNot.2: The project backlog holds epics for the whole project; a work package is a specific set of user stories.
whyNot.3: The team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts the work package, not by the PM.

B.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's store operations team uses Kanban and has no sprints. To forecast the remaining store roll-outs, project manager Patrick Dunne looks at how many stores have moved through preparation, training and go-live in recent weeks and projects that rate forward. Which planning concept is he applying?
options: Rationalism, predicting from reasoning
Magic estimation of the remaining stores
Empiricism, forecasting from actual rate
Trading stores of a similar size of effort
B.why: Empiricism bases decisions on what is happening or has happened: measure the rate of progress and forecast from it (8.3).

whyNot.0: Rationalism uses reasoning or logic to predict what should happen, rather than measured progress.
whyNot.1: Magic estimation sizes many items quickly before work; Patrick is using progress actually achieved.
whyNot.3: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb change; it is an issues technique, not a forecast.

B.q: Callowmere University's web team is about to create a story map for the Student Support Hub. Before brainstorming what users will do with the hub, the team needs a starting point that describes those users. What should the team start from?
options: The product breakdown structure from an earlier project
The task list in the team plan for the current sprint
Personas of the students who will use the hub
The cost and benefit figures in the project canvas
B.why: Story mapping starts from user descriptions or personas, then brainstorms user activities, orders them chronologically and breaks them into stories (8.3.2.4).

whyNot.0: The story map replaces the PBS, and an old project's PBS does not describe this hub's users.
whyNot.1: A team plan lists tasks for one iteration; it does not describe the users the story map serves.
whyNot.3: Costs and benefits justify the project; they do not describe users and their activities.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect project is in initiation. Project manager Patrick Dunne asks the board to approve a release map showing the three releases, their features, the budget and the tolerances. The detail of each sprint is left for the teams to plan nearer the time. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
options: Yes, because plans are made just in time at the right level
Yes, because the board approves each team plan in advance
No, because the board needs a Gantt chart to control time
No, because the release map should list each team's tasks
C.why: The release map is the high-level project plan with budget and tolerances; task-level planning is left until the team plans its next iteration, avoiding planning too early (8.3.2.5, Table 8.1).

whyNot.1: Team plans are produced by the teams when they accept work packages; the board does not approve them.
whyNot.2: Time is controlled through fixed timeboxes and the release map; a Gantt chart is not required.
whyNot.3: The release map shows releases and features; tasks belong in team plans for the next iteration.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's Repairs Reimagined project is in its first delivery stage. Repairs director Ian Thursby estimates every story for the service design team in hours, working on his own, and gives the figures to the team to plan with. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
options: Yes, because he manages the repairs contract and in-house team
Yes, because hour estimates suit work that is not software
No, because estimating is a task for the project board
No, because the whole team should estimate in relative terms
C.why: Agile estimating uses relative estimates and harnesses the whole team's knowledge so that everyone contributes without being swayed (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: He does manage the repairs contract and in-house team, but that does not make one person's estimates suitable for the team's planning.
whyNot.1: Relative, team-based estimating applies to any kind of product, not only to software.
whyNot.2: The board approves plans and tolerances; estimating stories is done by the delivery team.

C.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's Smart Maintenance project is at the end of Release 1. Andrea Lucas updates the release map for stage 3, forecasting how many machines each release can cover from the software team's average velocity in Release 1. Tasks for each sprint will be planned in team planning workshops. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
options: Yes, because it forecasts from the team's own measured rate
Yes, because the board approves team plans at a boundary
No, because one release is too little data to forecast from
No, because the release map should stay as it was approved
C.why: Empirical planning forecasts from the team's own measured velocity, and the stage boundary updates the high-level release map while task planning waits for each iteration (8.3, 8.3.2.5).

whyNot.1: Team plans are made by the delivery team in managing product delivery; the board approves the stage plan (release map).
whyNot.2: Empiricism means starting work and using the measured rate; data from a completed release is exactly what is needed.
whyNot.3: The release map is updated at stage boundaries with what has been learned; it is not frozen at initiation.

reteach.title: Judging a friend's house move plan
reteach.question: A friend is moving house in six weeks. Which parts of their plan are sensible, and which would you challenge?

blocks.body: A sensible plan lists the big milestones: book the van, pack the loft, change the address. It plans tomorrow's packing in detail. It estimates the rest from how many boxes they actually packed last weekend. It is not sensible to plan which mug goes in which box six weeks out, or to assume they will pack as fast as a removal company that does it every day.

blocks.text: A reason can be true and still not explain the verdict. 'Moving is stressful' is true, but it does not say why planning every mug six weeks early is a poor idea.

explain.body: At a stage boundary the plan is a release map: releases, features, timing, with budget and tolerances included or referenced. Task detail is left to the team plan for the next iteration.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's Care Online project is at the end of stage 2. Project manager Simon Archer updates the release map to show which features are expected in Release 2. The digital team will plan its tasks in each team planning workshop. How well does this apply the plans practice, and why?
options: Well, because detail is added just in time
Well, because the board approves the team plans
Poorly, because tasks belong in the stage plan
Poorly, because the release map is fixed at initiation
test.why: The release map is updated at a high level at the stage boundary, and the team adds task detail for each iteration in managing product delivery (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.1: Team plans are the delivery team's own plans; the board does not approve them.
whyNot.2: The stage plan is the release map, which stays at feature level; tasks belong in team plans.
whyNot.3: The release map is updated at each stage boundary as the project learns.

explain.body: A forecast should come from what this team has actually delivered. Borrowing another team's velocity, or one person's speed, does not reflect this team's work.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's data team has completed three sprints. To forecast its remaining work, the head of IT proposes using the speed of his fastest data scientist multiplied by the number of people in the team. What is the BEST reason to reject this?
options: Velocity should be the team's own measured rate
Forecasts must be approved by the project board
Story points can be converted into hours for this
The data team should be using Kanban instead
test.why: Empirical forecasting uses the team's own velocity, not another person's or team's rate (8.3).

whyNot.1: The board approves plans and tolerances, but that is not why this forecasting basis is poor.
whyNot.2: Agile estimates are relative; converting points to hours does not fix using one person's speed.
whyNot.3: The choice of agile approach is not the problem; the basis of the forecast is.

explain.body: Estimates are relative, not actual, and made by the whole team so that everyone contributes without being swayed by others. A manager handing down hour figures fails this test.

test.q: In Pinewick's team planning workshop, the e-commerce team's product owner announces her own size for each story first, and the team then agrees with her figure. What is the MAIN weakness of this estimating approach?
options: Story sizes should be set by the chief product owner
Estimates should be given in actual hours, not points
Team members are swayed by the first figure they hear
Estimating should wait until the stage boundary
test.why: Agile estimating should let everyone contribute without being prejudiced by others, for example by revealing estimates at the same moment (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: The CPO prioritizes across teams; sizing is a whole-team activity, not a CPO decision.
whyNot.1: PRINCE2 Agile uses relative estimates such as story points, not actual hours.
whyNot.3: Estimating stories for the next iteration is part of team planning in managing product delivery.

explain.h: Test 4: the reason must explain the case
explain.body: After deciding Yes or No, choose the reason that says why THIS approach fits or fails. A true statement that would apply to any project is usually the decoy.

test.q: Callowmere's project manager plans tasks for all sprints up to Welcome Week during initiation. You have decided this is NOT appropriate. Which reason BEST explains why?
options: Plans are approved by the board in directing a project
Detailed planning too early carries inherent risk
The web team uses Scrum with two-week sprints
Budgets in agile projects have zero cost tolerance
test.why: Agile plans are made just in time, because planning in detail too early carries inherent risks; tasks are planned for the next iteration (8.3.2.5).

whyNot.0: The board does approve plans, but that does not explain why task-level detail at initiation is poor.
whyNot.2: This is true of the team, but it does not explain why planning every sprint now is a poor choice.
whyNot.3: Cost tolerance is zero by default, but that is not the reason early task planning is inappropriate.
